paper.title: RDA: Reward Design Agent for Reinforcement Learning
paper.source_version: arXiv v1, submitted 2026-06-01; latest public arXiv version verified 2026-08-30; PDF SHA-256 6b93378f821f77497e2ad38d24826571af0f3ccd2c8282bc4f8c0c754ca0d256. The arXiv record says accepted to RLC 2026. Author project artifacts are pinned to commit 0b5c2ed3fed47084ae16b8bbbad23ffab0824301 (2026-05-13); that repository is not an end-to-end RDA implementation.

decision_relevance.why_admitted: RDA is direct evidence for iteratively editing executable task-reward code while holding a per-domain SAC/SimbaV2 learning setup fixed, using subtask-level visual trajectory diagnostics for search and a separate VLM plus benchmark success for reporting.
not_evidence_for: reference-clip composition, mode discovery, phase-window automata, or closed-loop oracle logic
runtime policy conditioning on a subtask, reference phase, or playback clock; explicit subtask-state conditioning is future work
a reward-only comparison under identical policy initialization, because the full loop may warm-start from the previous best checkpoint
an immutable search rubric across iterations, because subtask reflection changes the text used for candidate scoring
safe, sandboxed, or side-effect-free execution of generated reward code
end-to-end reproducibility from the public repository, which releases reward fragments and media but not the RDA loop or trainer
human-calibrated or physically objective instruction alignment from the GPT-4.1 pointwise evaluator
real-robot transfer or portability across controllers, trainers, observation contracts, dynamics, scenes, or budgets

mechanisms.name: Fixed-learner reward-design objective
mechanisms.description: The formal objective searches reward code R to maximize instruction score S(L(E,R),I) while the environment E, learning procedure L, instruction I, and scoring rule S are fixed for the problem instance.

mechanisms.name: Subtask-conditioned executable reward generation
mechanisms.description: GPT-5 decomposes the instruction using environment code and an image, then generates N environment-class reward functions as weighted sums of bounded subtask components, with explicit component logs and a terminal success bonus.

mechanisms.name: Subtask-level visual trajectory diagnostics
mechanisms.description: For each candidate, the agent VLM evaluates three rollout trajectories using frames and named reward-component values, assigns each ordered subtask a score in {0,0.5,1}, and produces behavior descriptions and failure rationales.

mechanisms.name: Visual-feedback evolutionary reward search
mechanisms.description: Each reward candidate trains a policy; mean VLM subtask score selects the iteration winner; its summary can revise one subtask and seeds N targeted reward-code revisions; the best reward across five iterations is returned.

mechanisms.name: Best-checkpoint policy warm-start
mechanisms.description: Candidate training may initialize from the previous iteration's best policy checkpoint; the component ablation treats checkpoint loading as a distinct intervention before visual analysis and subtask decomposition are added.

mechanisms.name: Separate alignment and success reporting
mechanisms.description: Search-time diagnostics use GPT-5 subtask scores, whereas reported alignment uses repeated pointwise GPT-4.1 video scores and reported success uses benchmark binary completion indicators.

mechanisms.name: Generated-reward artifact release
mechanisms.description: The pinned author repository exposes sixteen environment-dependent reward-function text fragments (twelve ManiSkill compute_dense_reward functions and four HumanoidBench get_reward functions) and policy media, but not the RDA generation, validation, training, rollout-analysis, selection, or checkpoint implementation.

failure_modes.name: Full-policy-training cost per candidate
failure_modes.description: The authors report that performance improves with more candidates, but every candidate requires a full RL training run; complete searches consume 20-40 GPU-hours per ManiSkill task and 240-360 per HumanoidBench task.

failure_modes.name: VLM diagnostic limits
failure_modes.description: The authors identify limited context, high inference cost, and imperfect fine-grained visual reasoning as constraints on diagnosis and reward revision.

failure_modes.name: Early-versus-late subtask reward conflict
failure_modes.description: In Humanoid Basketball, catching reward suppresses exploration of the later throwing behavior; the paper proposes explicit runtime subtask-state conditioning as future work rather than an implemented mechanism.

failure_modes.name: Reward and policy-initialization coupling
failure_modes.description: Optional warm-start from the previous best checkpoint changes policy initialization across reward generations; the checkpoint ablation changes alignment from 0.31 to 0.35 and success from 0.50 to 0.55, so full-loop effects are not reward-only under common initialization.

failure_modes.name: Uncalibrated pointwise alignment proxy
failure_modes.description: Reported alignment is repeated GPT-4.1 pointwise scoring without a reported human-agreement study; dividing the integer 1-5 scale by five yields support [0.2,1] although the paper calls it normalized to [0,1].

failure_modes.name: Mutable subtask selection rubric
failure_modes.description: The scoring procedure remains fixed, but subtask reflection changes the text used for subsequent trajectory scoring; the paper does not specify rescoring all candidates under one immutable rubric before returning the best reward across iterations.

failure_modes.name: Hyperparameter and iteration-reporting inconsistencies
failure_modes.description: The main text reports 2048 ManiSkill environments while the supplement reports 2000; package prose and its figure caption disagree on iteration indices; and the stated per-iteration GPU-hours do not arithmetically yield the reported five-iteration total ranges.

failure_modes.name: Generated-code validation and release gap
failure_modes.description: The paper says candidate code is compiled and validated but specifies no isolation or validation checks; the pinned repository supplies dependent reward fragments and media, not the RDA search/training implementation needed to inspect or reproduce that boundary.

evaluation.name: Separate VLM alignment and benchmark success protocol
evaluation.description: For each of three trained seeds, five videos receive four fixed-prompt GPT-4.1 scores on a 1-5 scale; sixty scores per task are averaged and divided by five. Success is the ManiSkill verifier or HumanoidBench terminal bonus interpreted as binary completion.

evaluation.name: ManiSkill aggregate comparison
evaluation.description: Across twelve tasks, RDA reports 0.95 alignment and 0.90 success, versus Eureka at 0.87 and 0.87, human dense at 0.68 and 0.74, and sparse at 0.28 and 0.17; RDA alone solves PlugCharger.

evaluation.name: HumanoidBench aggregate comparison
evaluation.description: Across four tasks, RDA reports 0.70 alignment and 0.42 success; Eureka alignment is 0.47 and RDA success is described as slightly lower; human rewards report 0.25 alignment and 0.08 success.

evaluation.name: Checkpoint, trajectory, and subtask component ablation
evaluation.description: On PlugCharger and Package over three seeds, Eureka scores 0.31/0.50 alignment/success; checkpoint loading gives 0.35/0.55; trajectory analysis gives 0.82/0.83; full RDA with subtask decomposition gives 0.84/1.00.

evaluation.name: Reward-candidate count scaling
evaluation.description: Increasing candidates from one to two to eight changes alignment/success from 0.46/0.20 to 0.58/0.51 to 0.84/1.00, while requiring correspondingly more full policy trainings.

evidence.locator: arXiv v1 metadata/header; submitted 2026-06-01; comment 'Accepted to RLC'26'
evidence.claim: The active v1 record gives the paper title, seven authors, submission date, and RLC 2026 acceptance note.
The objective searches reward R to maximize S(L(E,R),I) for a fixed environment, learning procedure, instruction, and score function.
RDA derives J ordered subtasks from the instruction and environment, generates N executable weighted reward programs, and says they are compiled and validated before search.

Each candidate trains a policy, yields K visual/logged rollouts, receives subtask scores and rationales, is selected by mean score, and supplies best reward, summary, and optional checkpoint feedback for subsequent revisions.
The reward prompt restricts code to existing environment fields, bounded [0,1] components, explicit weights, a summed scalar reward, a terminal bonus, and reward_-prefixed component logs.
Search-time analysis consumes frames and reward-component values, uses ordered subtask evaluation and scores {0,0.5,1}, and asks for behavior descriptions plus failure diagnoses.

evidence.locator: Supplement A.4-A.5, Subtask Reflection and Reward Reflection prompts
evidence.claim: Subtask reflection may edit one subtask without changing list length, and reward reflection makes a targeted code modification using the revised list, previous reward, success, and trajectory summary.

evidence.locator: Section 5.1, Tasks, Training, Evaluation, and Baselines
evidence.claim: The main setup uses GPT-5 medium, five iterations, SAC with SimbaV2, three seeds, 4/8 candidates, 50M/10M steps, 2048/16 environments, GPT-4.1 alignment, binary success, and matched Eureka settings.

evidence.locator: Supplement C, Table 1 and compute paragraph
evidence.claim: The table gives exact search, RL, agent-VLM, and evaluation-VLM parameters; the prose reports A100 hardware and 20-40 versus 240-360 GPU-hours per complete task search.

evidence.locator: Supplement D.1-D.2, Alignment Rate and Success Rate
evidence.claim: Five videos per policy are queried four times with GPT-4.1 for sixty scores per three-seed task, integer 1-5 scores are divided by five, and success uses benchmark binary indicators.
The paper reports aggregate RDA and baseline alignment/success on twelve ManiSkill and four HumanoidBench tasks, including reward-hacking behavior in the Eureka package policy.

evidence.locator: Section 5.3 and Figure 6, Humanoid Package evolution
evidence.claim: RDA diagnoses torso pushing instead of bilateral hand contact, revises the subtask, and gates hand-contact and box-forward reward terms on bilateral contact.
Three-seed ablations quantify checkpoint, visual trajectory, subtask-decomposition, and candidate-count effects on alignment and success for PlugCharger and Package.
The authors report per-candidate RL cost, VLM context/inference/visual limits, and conflict between catching and later throwing rewards; explicit subtask-state conditioning is future work.
RDA and baselines share SAC/SimbaV2, environment-step, candidate, model, reasoning, and instruction settings; Eureka receives numerical reward statistics rather than RDA visual diagnostics.

evidence.locator: Section 5.1 (2048 ManiSkill environments) versus Supplement C Table 1 (2000)
evidence.claim: The paper contains two different ManiSkill parallel-environment counts.

evidence.locator: Section 5.3 prose adjacent to Figure 6 versus Figure 6 caption
evidence.claim: Package prose says success after the second iteration and alignment 0.68 by iteration four, while the caption says success after the first and 0.68 at the fifth iteration.

evidence.locator: Author project repository tree at commit 0b5c2ed3fed47084ae16b8bbbad23ffab0824301, dated 2026-05-13
evidence.claim: The pinned tree contains sixteen reward text files plus project-page media and utilities, but no RDA generation, validation, policy-training, rollout-analysis, selection, or checkpoint implementation.
A released reward is a Python method fragment that depends on environment attributes, benchmark robot methods, NumPy, constants, and a success method; it is not standalone RDA code.
